To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the N metabolism of tree species with different flooding tolerances was affected differently by flooding, (ii) the N metabolism and N uptake of the flood tolerant poplars remained largely unaffected by flooding, (iii) in the flood tolerant poplar species, the N uptake and N-metabolites were affected to a lesser extent than in the flood tolerant oak species and (iv) the N-metabolic changes observed were correlated with the degree of flooding tolerance.
The impact of waterlogging on root N metabolism depends on the flooding tolerance of the tree species.
the effects of flooding on N metabolism of tree species vary distinctly, depending on their degree of flooding tolerance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of waterlogging on N metabolism in tree roots.
the effects of waterlogging on tree species and their N-metabolisms.
the effects of different flooding regimes on N uptake and metabolism of tree species of different degrees of flood tolerance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
flooding has a severe negative impact on the N-metabolic processes in the root system of flood intolerant tree species, which is reflected in a reduced N uptake and N assimilation.
the N-metabolic responses of the tree species studied are closely correlated with the degree of their flooding tolerance.
the N-metabolyism of poplar is not affected by flooding and that the effects of flooding on the N metabolism of oaks and beech are less severe than on poplars.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the flooding tolerance of tree species is correlated with their ability to maintain N uptake and N assimilation under waterlogged soil conditions and that this may be related to the ability to maintain root respiration.
flooding affects the metabolism of beech roots to a much larger degree than the metabolism of oaks and poplars.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the N‐metabolic responses of the tree species studied were highly correlated with their flooding tolerance, with the flood tolerant tree species exhibiting less negative impacts on the N‐status and N‐metabolisms of their roots than the flood sensitive tree species.
flooding affects the N metabolism in a species-specific manner and that this may be a major factor in determining the degree of tolerance of tree species to flooding.
